transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Thanks for seeing me. Well, to be honest, it’s getting to a point where I’m really struggling at work, and I just don't know what to do anymore. I'm a computer support specialist, and I deal with a lot of high-level IT infrastructure, which means I have to dig through a lot of data and solve complex issues. I have a graduate degree, so I know I'm capable of the work, but... well, what brings me in is that I just can't keep my mind on a task long enough to actually finish it anymore. 

It's like my brain just refuses to stay locked in. And the worst part is that this happens even when the task is incredibly important and people are actively relying on me to fix something. For example, I’ll start tracing a client's network problem—maybe their whole system is bottlenecking and it's an absolute emergency for their business—and I'll pull up the diagnostic logs to figure out where the issue is happening. I'll be sitting there, staring right at my monitors, and ten, maybe fifteen minutes later, I'll suddenly realize I've reread the exact same block of log entries three times. And I still don't know what they say! 

It's like my eyes are scanning the text, the words are right there in front of me, but absolutely nothing is registering in my brain. I just sit there looking at the screen, and my mind has completely slipped off the task. It takes me forever to get through something that should be routine because I have to keep dragging my attention back to the exact same line of text, over and over. It’s incredibly frustrating to want to do the work, to know it's urgent, and just... not be able to hold onto the thread long enough to get to the end of it.
Have you experienced this kind of trouble sustaining attention since you were a child, or is this a new change compared to how your mind used to work?

Well, no, it’s definitely not new. Not at all. I mean, if you ask my mother—she's in her late seventies now, and she actually still brings this up, which is a little funny but also sort of frustrating when you're fifty-three years old—she still jokes about my old grade school report cards. She kept them all in this old box, and it’s almost a running family joke at this point. 

Because every single one of those report cards, from first grade all the way up, basically said the exact same thing. The teachers would always write these long notes in the margins saying that I was a very bright kid, that I had a lot of potential and clearly understood the material, but... well, there was always a big 'but' attached to it. They'd complain that I absolutely never stayed in my seat. I was just constantly up and wandering around the classroom, going to the pencil sharpener for the fifth time, or just getting up for no reason at all. And I couldn't just sit quietly and wait my turn, either. If the teacher asked a question, I would just blurt the answer right out. I wouldn't even think to raise my hand, the words would just fly out of my mouth the second they popped into my head. 

And the homework... oh, man, the homework was just a disaster. The most ridiculous part was that I actually *did* the assignments. I’d sit at the kitchen table and finish the math sheets or whatever it was, but then somewhere between my house and the classroom the next morning, it would just disappear. I’d lose it entirely. I’d shove it in the wrong folder, or leave it on the bus, or it would just vanish into the black hole at the bottom of my backpack. 

So, yeah, this... this feeling of just not being able to keep things on track or stay locked in, it’s been happening my whole life. It's just that now, instead of losing a third-grade spelling sheet or wandering around a classroom, I'm losing the thread on critical IT infrastructure, you know? It just has much bigger consequences now.
Aside from your struggles at work, do you notice these same problems with focus, restlessness, or impulsivity affecting other areas of your life—like at home, in social situations, or when driving?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because... well, actually, I'm not entirely sure. I mean, I guess I haven't really stopped to think about how it bleeds into other things, mostly because work is just taking up so much of my mental energy right now. It’s like, when the IT stuff is constantly on the verge of catching fire, that’s where the spotlight is, you know? 

At home, I mean... I don't know if I'd say I have those exact same problems. My wife handles a lot of the day-to-day organization around the house, bless her, so maybe she's just buffering me from noticing it? I mean, sure, I might start a project in the garage and then leave the tools out for a week because I got sidetracked by something in the yard, but isn't that just... normal? Like, doesn't everyone do that to some extent? 

And socially... I don't really know. We don't go out to big parties or anything. Usually it's just dinner with a few friends, and I feel like I hold my own in a conversation, though I suppose I do have a habit of jumping in when I get excited about a topic, especially if it's tech-related or something I've been reading about. But I wouldn't call it a major problem, or at least, nobody's ever pulled me aside and told me I was being too impulsive or anything like that. 

As for driving... well, I commute about forty-five minutes each way, and honestly, I just put on a podcast or an audiobook, usually something pretty dense about history or economics, and just kind of zone out until I pull into the parking lot. I haven't had any accidents or anything, if that's what you mean. So, yeah, I really couldn't say for sure if it's happening outside of work. It's really just the job that's pushing me to the brink right now. The job is where the wheels are really coming off.

Can you tell me about a specific recent time at home—like paying bills, managing household paperwork, or finishing a chore—where you noticed your mind wandering or losing track partway through, similar to what happens at work?

Well, now that you mention paying bills, it actually reminds me of something that happened just recently, and it really gets to the heart of what you're asking. I know I said earlier that my wife handles most of the household organization, like the mortgage and the electric bill, but I do take care of the tech-specific stuff for the house. For instance, we have a family cloud backup account. It holds literally everything—all our digital photos from the last fifteen years, scanned tax documents, my wife's graduate thesis, just everything. 

Well, the credit card on file expired. I got the notification email—I actually distinctly remember looking at the email on my phone while I was standing in the kitchen making coffee. I told myself, 'Okay, the second I sit down with my laptop, I will update that billing info.' But then I noticed a loose hinge on the kitchen cabinet door, decided I needed to tighten it right then and there so it wouldn't get worse, walked out to the garage to find a Phillips head screwdriver... and the bill completely vanished from my mind. Just gone. I completely forgot to pay the cloud backup bill until two weeks later when we got a final notice that they were going to suspend the account and potentially purge all our data. 

And it’s not just bills, either. It’s... it’s just ordinary but really important things, all the time. Like, I do this volunteer class on Thursday evenings at the local community center. I teach basic computer and internet safety to seniors, which is a really wonderful program, but they rely on me to have the right equipment to actually show them what I'm doing. Last week, I knew I needed to bring a specific USB-C to HDMI adapter so

Besides that cloud backup bill, can you think of another recent example at home or in your personal life—outside of work—where this kind of forgetfulness or losing track of things caused a real problem, like missing an appointment or misplacing something important?

Well, right, exactly, that’s actually what I was just trying to explain about the volunteer class! Because that’s a perfect example of how this messes up my personal life. Like I was saying, I needed this specific USB-C to HDMI adapter to hook my laptop up to the projector at the community center. I had it in my hand. I specifically remember holding it while I was putting on my shoes. But then the dog started barking at a delivery truck outside, so I set the adapter down on the entryway table to go check the window, and... well, you can guess the rest. I grabbed my keys and walked right out the door without it.

I didn't realize until I was standing in front of fifteen seniors who were all looking at me, waiting to learn about password managers, and I couldn't connect my screen to the projector. I felt like an absolute idiot. I had to try and explain two-factor authentication using just my hands and a squeaky dry-erase marker, which, let me tell you, does not work well for an eighty-year-old who barely uses a smartphone. 

It’s just... it’s a constant cycle. I forget these ordinary but incredibly important things all the time—whether it’s bringing the right adapter to a volunteer class, or paying that cloud backup bill I mentioned, or even just returning a freelance client's call when I do a little side consulting on the weekends. I have every intention of doing the thing, but it just slips through the cracks of my brain the second a distraction happens. 

And then I spend the entire next day just... apologizing. Just apologizing over and over, sending embarrassing emails, making excuses, and frantically trying to patch the damage I caused. The seniors were actually incredibly sweet about the whole adapter situation, which honestly almost made me feel worse, you know? Because I'm fifty-three years old. I shouldn't be letting people down over something as simple as remembering to put a cable in my bag. But it just keeps happening, and it's exhausting trying to constantly clean up my own messes.
